q: Tomorrow's forecast for your area is northwest force 7. What does that mean for your 12 m charter yacht?
a: Near gale, 28–33 kn — stay in harbour
o: Moderate breeze, 11–16 kn — full sail
Fresh breeze, 17–21 kn — one reef
Strong breeze, 22–27 kn — two reefs
why: Force 7 is a near gale, 28–33 knots: more than a flotilla boat should go out in.

q: Your flotilla is in the Cyclades in August and the lead crew warns of the Meltemi. Where will it blow from?
a: From the north
o: From the south
From the west
From the east
why: The Meltemi is the Aegean's summer northerly: NE in the north, N in the Cyclades, NW in the Dodecanese.

q: This is tomorrow's forecast chart, and you are where the boat is drawn. What wind do you expect?
a: Strong wind — the isobars are packed close
o: Light wind — you are near the centre of the low
Light wind — close isobars mean a calm area
No change — isobars show pressure, not wind
why: The closer together the isobars, the stronger the wind.

q: You are in a remote Ionian anchorage with no phone signal. How do you get tomorrow's official forecast?
a: Listen to the coast station's VHF broadcasts or read NAVTEX
o: Call the coastguard on channel 16 and ask for it
Read the barometer and the clouds — that is enough
Use yesterday's forecast — it covers three days
why: Coast stations broadcast forecasts and warnings on VHF at set times; NAVTEX prints them aboard.

q: You must make this leg today. When do you go?
a: At first light, to arrive before midday
o: After lunch, once the wind has settled
In the late afternoon, when the peak has passed
At midday, when the morning breeze has gone
why: The Meltemi is usually lightest in the early morning and strongest in the afternoon.

fig.title: Meltemi forecast
lines: Your leg: 15 M north to the next island

q: Your crew hopes it will blow itself out overnight. How do you plan?
a: Expect it to last — sheltered legs only, or stay put
o: Go at dawn — it always dies after one day
Go tomorrow afternoon, once it has peaked
Go now — it will only get worse later
why: A Meltemi often blows for days: plan on the forecast, not on hope, and ask the lead crew for a sheltered route.

fig.title: Cyclades, late July
lines: Forecast: the same for 3 more days

q: It is a calm, sunny July morning in the Ionian. What wind do you plan on for the afternoon?
a: A northwest breeze, building to about force 4
o: Calm all day — sunny days bring no wind
A south wind, building through the night
A gale — a calm morning comes before a storm
why: In summer the Ionian's northwesterly builds from late morning and dies away around sunset.

q: You are anchored off a beach on a hot, settled day. In the early afternoon a breeze sets in from the sea. What does it mean for you?
a: It blows onshore — the beach is now a lee shore
o: It blows offshore — the beach gives you shelter
It will die within minutes — sea breezes are brief
A front is coming — expect rain by evening
why: On hot days the sea breeze blows from sea to land, putting boats off a beach on a lee shore until evening.

q: You are choosing where to anchor for the night in this bay. Where do you go?
a: B — well clear of the valley mouth
o: A — right off the valley, closest to the beach
Either — the gusts hit the whole bay equally
Mid-bay, as far from the land as you can
why: At night gusts pour down valleys off high land; anchor away from the valley mouth.

fig.note: Pilot book: violent gusts down the valley at night

q: The cloud will reach you before you reach harbour. What do you do with the sails now?
a: Reef or drop sail now, before the squall arrives
o: Keep full sail and race the cloud to harbour
Wait for the first gust, then decide
Head out to sea, away from the lightning
why: Thunderstorms bring sudden violent squalls; reduce sail before they hit, not during.

fig.title: Late afternoon, August
lines: Tall dark cloud building over the mainland
Thunder heard, the cloud is coming your way
4 M to harbour, full sail set

q: You are anchored here for the night. What does the forecast mean for you?
a: The wind swings into the open west — move before dark
o: The wind swings to the east — better shelter still
Nothing — veering changes only the wind's strength
It falls calm — veering means the wind dies away
why: Veering is a clockwise shift: south to west turns this bay into a lee shore.

q: You are in harbour planning tomorrow's leg. What do these readings suggest?
a: A low is approaching — expect the wind to rise
o: A high is building — settled weather to come
A normal daily swing — nothing to note
The wind will drop — a falling glass means calm
why: A steady fall of 1 hPa an hour with thickening cloud points to a low and stronger wind.

fig.title: Barometer log
lines: Sky: high cloud thickening from the west

q: You read the wind instrument before slipping your lines. How do you set up the boat?
a: Force 5 — take in a reef before you go
o: Force 3 — shake out every reef, full sail
Force 7 — stay in harbour, a near gale
Force 9 — stay in and double the lines
why: 18 kn mean is force 5 (17–21 kn); reef in harbour, not out in the gusts.

fig.title: Wind instrument at the quay
lines: Your leg: 12 M on a beam reach
Crew: two who have sailed before

q: Tomorrow's chart puts you here, under this pattern. What do you plan for the day?
a: Light winds — plan to motor part of the way
o: A gale — stay in harbour all day
Strong winds — reef before you leave
Thunderstorms — a high always brings them
why: Widely spaced isobars round a high mean light winds; allow time and fuel for motoring.

q: You are deciding whether to sail today. What do you choose?
a: Stay in harbour — it is too much for this crew
o: Leave now under full sail to beat the rise
Leave at midday, once the wind has peaked
Leave now and reef only when it reaches 7
why: 14 M upwind takes over four hours, into force 6–7 with a new crew: the safe call is to stay.

q: The forecast reads: 'Northwest 4 to 5, locally 6.' Your route rounds a high cape and goes through a channel between islands. What do you expect there?
a: Force 6 in places — round capes and in channels
o: Force 6 only at night, when the land cools
Force 6 only far offshore, out of sight of land
Force 6 for a few minutes in every hour
why: 'Locally' means stronger in places — typically where the wind is squeezed round capes and between islands.

q: The marine forecast gives 'wind 15 knots, gusts 25 knots' for your afternoon leg. What do you set your sails for?
a: The 25 kn gusts, not the 15 kn mean
o: The 15 kn mean — gusts pass quickly
Full sail — gusts are only felt at anchor
A reef for 15 kn, shaken out in the gusts
why: Your sail plan must cope with the gusts, and 25 kn is already force 6.

q: You are sailing with the VHF on channel 16 and hear a SÉCURITÉ call announcing a gale warning on another channel. What do you do?
a: Switch to the channel given and listen to the warning
o: Reply on 16 to confirm you have heard it
Ignore it — gale warnings are for ships
Wait for the full warning to be read on 16
why: SÉCURITÉ is announced on 16 and read out on a working channel: switch over, listen, then go back to 16.

q: Your crew prefers the phone app. Which forecast do you plan on?
a: The official one — plan for force 6–7
o: The app — it is more detailed for your spot
An average of the two — plan for force 5
The app, unless the barometer starts to fall
why: Plan on the official forecast and warnings, and on the worse of two forecasts that disagree.

fig.title: Two forecasts for tomorrow
lines: NAVTEX: warning, NW 7 in your area

q: Your crew says nothing can blow from a sky like this. Are they right?
a: No — the Meltemi blows hard under clear skies
o: Yes — strong wind always comes with cloud
Yes — a steady barometer means light winds
Only if the barometer starts to fall later
why: The Meltemi is a fair-weather wind: clear sky, steady barometer, and still force 6–7.

fig.title: Paros, early August
lines: Sky clear blue, not a cloud
